analysis.investment_thesis: Fabtech fails the Magic Formula test: earnings yield of ~6% (EBIT 16 Cr / EV ~260 Cr) is well below my 12% threshold, and while ROCE of 21% is decent, it's not exceptional enough to justify a P/E of 27.6. Cheap + good is what I want; this is moderately good but decidedly not cheap.
key_strengths: ROCE of 21.2% and ROE of 18.1% — acceptable capital efficiency
EBIT CAGR of 21.7% and net profit CAGR of 26.6% over 5 years
Low leverage (borrowings 10 Cr vs equity 95 Cr) and 5/5 years positive OCF
key_risks: Earnings yield ~6% (EBIT 16 / EV ~260) — expensive on Magic Formula basis
FCF collapsed to 0 Cr in 2025 despite 13 Cr net profit — poor cash conversion
Small-cap cyclical order book (turnkey engineering) with lumpy revenue (70→114→125→97→150)
red_flags: Investing CF of -26 Cr in 2025 funded by 24 Cr financing inflow (likely IPO) — ROCE may dilute as fresh capital deploys
FY25 OCF of only 3 Cr vs reported PAT of 13 Cr — working capital absorbing earnings
analysis.detailed_analysis: Running the Magic Formula: EBIT of 16 Cr against an enterprise value of roughly 260 Cr (market cap 270 + debt 10 - est. cash ~20 from IPO proceeds) gives an earnings yield near 6.2% — materially below my 12% minimum. ROCE at 21.2% is respectable but not top-decile, and my own EBIT/Capital Employed calculation (16/~105 Cr) comes in closer to 15%, suggesting the reported figure flatters itself with pre-IPO capital base. This is a mediocre ranking on both axes combined.\n\nThe business itself — turnkey cleanrooms for pharma — has decent tailwinds and the earnings trajectory (PAT 4→13 Cr) is encouraging, but the 27.6x P/E already prices in continued execution. More troubling for a systematic buyer: FCF was 0 Cr in 2025 despite 13 Cr of reported profit, and the recent equity raise will dilute return on capital until deployed. The Magic Formula rewards cheap-and-good; Fabtech is fairly-good-and-expensive. Pass.
